claim: Neuroanatomical structures within the medial temporal lobe (MTL) are known to support memory-related behaviors.
source: Neuroanatomical structures within the medial temporal lobe (MTL) are known to support memory-related behaviors (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2004; LaRocque and Wagner, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on MTL and memory.

claim: Experimentalists have observed MTL-related impairments in tasks designed to test perceptual processing.
source: For decades, experimentalists have also observed MTL-related impairments in tasks designed to test perceptual processing (Suzuki, 2009; Baxter, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Perirhinal cortex (PRC) is an MTL structure situated at the apex of high-level sensory cortices.
source: These findings centered on perirhinal cortex (PRC), an MTL structure situated at the apex of high-level sensory cortices (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1a showing anatomical location.

claim: Visual impairments were reported following lesions to PRC in humans and other animals.
source: Visual impairments were reported following lesions to PRC in humans and other animals, bolstering a perceptual-mnemonic account of perirhinal function (e.g. Murray and Bussey, 1999; Bussey et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2006; Barense et al., 2007; Inhoff et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: There were visual experiments for which no impairments were observed following PRC lesions.
source: However, there were also visual experiments for which no impairments were observed following PRC lesions (e.g. Buffalo et al., 1998a; Buffalo et al., 1998b; Stark and Squire, 2000; Knutson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies showing no impairments.

claim: Decades of evidence resulted in a pattern of seemingly inconsistent experimental outcomes regarding PRC function.
source: In this was, decades of evidence resulted in a pattern of seemingly inconsistent experimental outcomes, with no formal method for disambiguating between competing interpretations of the available data.
evidence: Inferred from the summary of conflicting experimental results cited.

claim: One central challenge has been isolating PRC-dependent behaviors from those supported by PRC-adjacent sensory cortex.
source: One of the central challenges in this experimental literature has been isolating PRC-dependent behaviors from those supported by PRC-adjacent sensory cortex.
evidence: Stated as a challenge in the field based on the experimental context.

claim: In the primate, isolating PRC-dependent behaviors requires disentangling PRC-dependent performance from visual behaviors supported by the ventral visual stream (VVS).
source: In the primate, this requires disentangling PRC-dependent performance from visual behaviors supported by the ventral visual stream (VVS; DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; DiCarlo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on the VVS.

claim: Experimentalists had relied on informal, descriptive accounts of perceptual demands such as 'complexity' and 'feature ambiguity'.
source: Lacking more objective metrics, experimentalists had relied on informal, descriptive accounts of perceptual demands; terms such as 'complexity' and 'feature ambiguity' were intended to characterize those stimulus properties that are necessary to evaluate PRC involvement in visual object perception.
evidence: Describes the historical approach in the field.

claim: The informal approach to characterizing perceptual demands led to conflicting interpretations of the available evidence.
source: However, this informal approach led to conflicting interpretations of the available evidence, without any means to arbitrate between them.
evidence: Inferred from the description of the problem in the field.

claim: Deep learning computational methods have become commonplace in the vision sciences in recent years.
source: In recent years, deep learning computational methods have become commonplace in the vision sciences.
evidence: General knowledge about the field's recent developments.

claim: Deep learning models are able to predict neural responses throughout the primate VVS directly from experimental stimuli.
source: Remarkably, these models are able to predict neural responses throughout the primate VVS directly from experimental stimuli: given an experimental image as input, these models (e.g. convolutional neural networks, CNNs) are able to predict neural responses.
evidence: Describes the capability of CNNs based on established research.

claim: Stimulus-computable methods currently provide the most quantitatively accurate predictions of neural responses throughout the primate VVS.
source: These 'stimulus-comptable' methods currently provide the most quantitatively accurate predictions of neural responses throughout the primate VVS (Yamins et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Rajalingham et al., 2018; Bashivan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to computational neuroscience studies.

claim: Early model layers within a CNN better predict earlier stages of processing within the VVS (e.g. V4).
source: For example, early model layers within a CNN better predict earlier stages of processing within the VVS (e.g. V4; Figure 1b: left, gray) while later model layers better predict later stages of processing within the VVS (e.g. IT; Figure 1b: left, green).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1b with data.

claim: Later model layers better predict later stages of processing within the VVS (e.g. IT).
source: For example, early model layers within a CNN better predict earlier stages of processing within the VVS (e.g. V4; Figure 1b: left, gray) while later model layers better predict later stages of processing within the VVS (e.g. IT; Figure 1b: left, green).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1b with data.

claim: There is not a 1–1 correspondence between CNN models and the primate VVS as they typically lack known biological properties.
source: We note that there is not a 1–1 correspondence between these models and the primate VVS as they typically lack known biological properties (Zhuang et al., 2021; Doerig et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations discussing model limitations.

claim: CNN models can be modified to evaluate domain-specific hypotheses.
source: Nonetheless, these models can be modified to evaluate domain-specific hypotheses (Doerig et al., 2022)—for example by adding recurrence (Kubilius et al., 2018; Kietzmann et al., 2019) or eccentricity-dependent scaling (Deza and Konkle, 2020; Jonnalagadda et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies modifying CNNs.

claim: Bonnen et al., 2021 leveraged VVS-like models to evaluate the performance of PRC-intact/-lesioned human participants in visual discrimination tasks.
source: Recently, Bonnen et al., 2021 leveraged these 'VVS-like' models to evaluate the performance of PRC-intact/-lesioned human participants in visual discrimination tasks.
evidence: Cites a specific study and its approach.

claim: VVS-like models are able to approximate performance supported by a linear readout of high-level visual cortex.
source: While VVS-like models are able to approximate performance supported by a linear readout of high-level visual cortex (Figure 1b: right, green), human participants are able to out outperform both VVS-like models and a linear readout of direct electrophysiological recordings from the VVS (Figure 1b: right, purple).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Human participants are able to outperform both VVS-like models and a linear readout of direct electrophysiological recordings from the VVS.
source: While VVS-like models are able to approximate performance supported by a linear readout of high-level visual cortex (Figure 1b: right, green), human participants are able to out outperform both VVS-like models and a linear readout of direct electrophysiological recordings from the VVS (Figure 1b: right, purple).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1b with data from Bonnen et al., 2021.

claim: VVS-like models approximate PRC-lesioned performance.
source: Critically, VVS-like models approximate PRC-lesioned performance.
evidence: Stated as a critical finding from Bonnen et al., 2021.

claim: The data from Bonnen et al., 2021 implicate PRC in visual object processing.
source: Critically, VVS-like models approximate PRC-lesioned performance. While these data implicate PRC in visual object processing, there remains experimental data collected from non-human primates which have not been formally evaluated.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that models approximate lesioned but not intact performance.

claim: Non-human primate data have been used to both support and refute PRC involvement in perception.
source: Like the human literature, non-human primate data have been used to both support and refute PRC involvement in perception.
evidence: Describes the state of the literature.

claim: Experiments with non-human primates have unparalleled control over the site and extent of PRC lesions.
source: Unlike the naturally occurring lesioned in humans, experiments with non-human primates have unparalleled control over the site and extent of PRC lesions—potentially, providing more incisive tests of competing claims over PRC function.
evidence: Describes an advantage of non-human primate research.

claim: Characterizing the discrepancies between human and non-human primate data is a critical step toward developing a more formal understanding of PRC involvement in perception.
source: As such, characterizing the discrepancies between human and non-human primate data is a critical step toward developing a more formal understanding of PRC involvement in perception.
evidence: Stated as a motivation for the current study.

claim: Eldridge et al., 2018 provides striking evidence against PRC involvement in perception.
source: We draw from data collected by Eldridge et al., 2018 which provides striking evidence against PRC involvement in perception: Eldridge et al., 2018 created multiple stimulus sets, allowing for more a fine-grained evaluation of perceptual behaviors than previous, related work (e.g. Bussey et al., 2003).
evidence: Describes the original interpretation of Eldridge et al., 2018.

claim: Eldridge et al., 2018 created multiple stimulus sets, allowing for more fine-grained evaluation of perceptual behaviors than previous work.
source: Eldridge et al., 2018 created multiple stimulus sets, allowing for more a fine-grained evaluation of perceptual behaviors than previous, related work (e.g. Bussey et al., 2003).
evidence: Describes a methodological feature of the cited study.

claim: To evaluate PRC involvement in perception, the performance of non-lesioned participants must exceed VVS-modeled performance.
source: That is, supra-VVS performance must be observed in order to isolate PRC contributions from those of other possible contributors to these behaviors (e.g. prefrontal cortex, schematized in Figure 1c: center).
evidence: Stated as a criterion based on the modeling framework and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: VVS-like models are suitable proxies for VVS-supported performance.
source: These data suggest that while these models are suitable proxies for VVS-supported performance, human performance is able to exceed a linear readout of the VVS.
evidence: Inferred from the correspondence between model and VVS performance.

claim: Human performance is able to exceed a linear readout of the VVS.
source: These data suggest that while these models are suitable proxies for VVS-supported performance, human performance is able to exceed a linear readout of the VVS.
evidence: Supported by the statistical comparison showing humans outperform VVS.

claim: Subjects in Eldridge et al., 2018 provided a binary classification for each stimulus: 'cat' or 'dog'.
source: In these experiments, subjects provided a binary classification for each stimulus: 'cat' or 'dog.'
evidence: Describes the experimental task from Eldridge et al., 2018.

claim: Stimuli in Eldridge et al., 2018 were composed of cats, dogs, and 'morphed' images that parametrically vary the percent of category-relevant information.
source: Critically, stimuli were composed not only of cats and dogs, but of 'morphed' images that parametrically vary the percent of category-relevant information present in each trial.
evidence: Describes the stimulus design from Eldridge et al., 2018.

claim: Morphed stimuli were designed to evaluate PRC involvement in perception by creating maximal 'feature ambiguity'.
source: These morphed stimuli were designed to evaluate PRC involvement in perception by creating maximal 'feature ambiguity,' a perceptual quality reported to elicit PRC dependence in previous work (Bussey et al., 2002; Norman and Eacott, 2004; Bussey et al., 2006; Murray and Richmond, 2001).
evidence: Describes the rationale for stimulus design with citations to previous work.

claim: Subjects were rewarded for responses that correctly identify which category best fits the image presented.
source: On each trial, subjects were rewarded for responses that correctly identify which category best fits the image presented (e.g. 10% = 'cat', 90% = 'dog', correct response is 'dog').
evidence: Describes the reward structure of the task.

claim: The study evaluated data from an unoperated control group (n = 3) and a group with bilateral removal of rhinal cortex (n = 3).
source: We evaluate data from two groups of monkeys in this study: an unoperated control group (n = 3) and a group with bilateral removal of rhinal cortex, which including peri- and entorhinal cortex.
evidence: Describes the experimental groups from Eldridge et al., 2018.

claim: A computational proxy for the VVS exhibits the same qualitative pattern of behavior as each subject group.
source: A computational proxy for the VVS exhibits the same qualitative pattern of behavior as each subject group (Figure 2c, model performance across multiple train–test iterations in black).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 2c.

claim: A linear readout of the VVS appears to be sufficient to perform these tasks.
source: As such, a linear readout of the VVS appears to be sufficient to perform these tasks, thus there need be no involvement of PRC to achieve neurotypical performance.
evidence: Inferred from the correspondence between VVS model and both lesioned and intact performance.

claim: There need be no involvement of PRC to achieve neurotypical performance on these tasks.
source: As such, a linear readout of the VVS appears to be sufficient to perform these tasks, thus there need be no involvement of PRC to achieve neurotypical performance.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that VVS models match both intact and lesioned performance.

claim: Experimental stimuli contain discrete interpolations between 'cat' and 'dog' images, such that adjacent stimuli within a morph sequence are highly similar.
source: Experimental stimuli contain discrete interpolations between 'cat' and 'dog' images, such that adjacent stimuli within a morph sequence are highly similar (e.g. see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Describes a property of the stimulus set with reference to figure.

claim: The correspondence between VVS models and primate choice behaviors is not an artifact of low-level stimulus attributes.
source: That is, although subjects were able to exploit the colinearity in the stimuli to improve their performance with experience, the correspondence between VVS models and primate choice behaviors is not an artifact of these low-level stimulus attributes.
evidence: Inferred from the conservative analysis showing VVS models still predict behavior when pixel-level features do not.

claim: These models approximate neural responses and choice behaviors in the aggregate but do not necessarily capture trial-by-trial choice behaviors.
source: This is an important caveat to note when evaluating the correspondence between model performance and animal behavior: as previously reported (Rajalingham et al., 2018), even as these models approximate neural responses and choice behaviors in the aggregate (i.e. across images), they do not necessarily capture the trial-by-trial choice behaviors.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and current findings.

claim: The absence of PRC-related deficits across four experiments led the original authors to suggest that perceptual processing is not dependent on PRC.
source: The absence of PRC-related deficits across four experiments led the original authors to suggest that perceptual processing is not dependent on PRC.
evidence: Describes the conclusion from Eldridge et al., 2018.

claim: VVS-model performance predicts both PRC-intact and -lesioned choice behaviors in Eldridge et al., 2018.
source: We first determined VVS-model performance on the experimental stimuli in Eldridge et al., 2018. We then compared these computational results with monkey choice behaviors, including subjects with bilateral lesions to PRC (n = 3), as well as unoperated controls (n = 3). For both PRC-lesioned/-intact monkeys, we observe a striking correspondence between VVS model and experimental behavior at the group (Figure 2d) and subject level (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by the analyses presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: A linear readout of the VVS should be sufficient to enable the visual classification behaviors in Eldridge et al., 2018.
source: These results suggest that a linear readout of the VVS should be sufficient to enable the visual classification behaviors in Eldridge et al., 2018; no PRC-related impairments are expected.
evidence: Inferred from the correspondence between VVS models and both intact and lesioned performance.

claim: No PRC-related impairments are expected in the tasks from Eldridge et al., 2018.
source: These results suggest that a linear readout of the VVS should be sufficient to enable the visual classification behaviors in Eldridge et al., 2018; no PRC-related impairments are expected.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that VVS models match both intact and lesioned performance.

claim: For a stimulus set to evaluate PRC involvement in visual processing, participants must be able to outperform a linear readout of the VVS.
source: Because results from these human experiments are in the same metric space as our current results (i.e. VVS-modeled performance), these data unambiguously constrain our interpretation: for a stimulus set to evaluate PRC involvement in visual processing, participants must be able to outperform a linear readout of the VVS.
evidence: Inferred from the framework established by comparing human and model performance.

claim: Supra-VVS performance must be observed in order to isolate PRC contributions from those of other possible contributors.
source: That is, supra-VVS performance must be observed in order to isolate PRC contributions from those of other possible contributors to these behaviors (e.g. prefrontal cortex, schematized in Figure 1c: center).
evidence: Stated as a criterion for evaluating PRC involvement and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Experiments in Eldridge et al., 2018 are not diagnostic of PRC involvement in perception.
source: Given that supra-VVS performance is not observed in the current stimulus set (Figure 2d; schematized in Figure 1c: right), we conclude that experiments in Eldridge et al., 2018 are not diagnostic of PRC involvement in perception.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that VVS models match intact performance, illustrated in Figures 1c and 2d.

claim: Data from Eldridge et al., 2018 do not offer absolute evidence against PRC involvement in perception.
source: Consequently, we suggest that these data do not offer absolute evidence against PRC involvement in perception—revising the original conclusions made from this study.
evidence: Stated as a revision of the original interpretation based on the modeling results.

claim: There is meaningful variance in the trial-level behaviors not captured by the current modeling framework.
source: We note that there is meaningful variance in the trial-level behaviors not captured by the current modeling framework.
evidence: Stated as a limitation based on the image-level analysis.

claim: Image-level choice behaviors are reliable both within and between subjects.
source: By conducting a more granular analyses than the original study (i.e. an image-level analysis, instead of averaging across multiple images within the same morph level), we found that image-level choice behaviors are reliable both within and between subjects (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by split-half reliability analysis and illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: At the image-level resolution, the VVS model does not match the pattern of choice behaviors evident in experimental subjects.
source: At this image-level resolution, however, the VVS model does not match the pattern of choice behaviors evident in experimental subjects (Figure 3c Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by the consistency analysis and illustrated in Figure 3c.

claim: VVS-like models are best suited to approximate aggregate choice behaviors, not responses to individual images.
source: This observation is consistent with previous reports (Rajalingham et al., 2018), suggesting that these VVS-like models are best suited to approximate aggregate choice behaviors, not responses to individual images.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and current findings.

claim: Many sources of variance have been identified as possible contributors to subject–model divergences, such as biologically implausible training data or lack of known properties of the primate visual system.
source: Many sources of variance have been identified as possible contributors to these subject–model divergences, such as biologically implausible training data (Zhuang et al., 2021), or lack of known properties of the primate visual system—for example recurrence (Kar and DiCarlo, 2020) or eccentricity-dependent scaling (Jonnalagadda et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on model limitations.

claim: Computational proxies for the VVS provide an unprecedented opportunity to understand perirhinal function.
source: While admittedly coarse, these computational proxies for the VVS provide an unprecedented opportunity to understand perirhinal function.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion about the value of the modeling approach.

claim: The principal contribution of these computational methods is to isolate PRC-dependent behaviors from those supported by the VVS.
source: Their contribution is, principally, to isolate PRC-dependent behaviors from those supported by the VVS.
evidence: Stated as the main contribution of the modeling approach.

claim: The stimulus-computable property of these models provides a formal 'linking function' between theoretical claims with experimental evidence.
source: This stimulus-computable property of these models provides a formal 'linking function' between theoretical claims with experimental evidence.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the modeling approach.

claim: This modeling approach creates a unified metric space that enables evaluation of experimental outcomes across labs, studies, and species.
source: In turn, this modeling approach creates a unified metric space (in this case, 'model performance') that enables us to evaluate experimental outcomes across labs, across studies, and even across species.
evidence: Stated as a benefit of the modeling framework.

claim: A judicious application of these computational tools, alongside careful consideration of animal behavior, will enrich the next generation of empirical studies surrounding MTL-dependent perceptual processing.
source: We believe that a judicious application of these computational tools, alongside a careful consideration of animal behavior, will enrich the next generation of empirical studies surrounding MTL-dependent perceptual processing.
evidence: Stated as a forward-looking conclusion.

claim: The study used a task-optimized convolutional neural network pretrained on Imagenet.
source: For all estimates of model performance we use a task-optimized convolutional neural network pretrained on Imagenet (Deng et al., 2009).
evidence: Describes the model used in the methods.

claim: The study used electrophysiological responses previously collected from macaque VVS.
source: Using previously collected electrophysiological responses from macaque VVS (Majaj et al., 2015), we identify a model layer that best fits high-level visual cortex
evidence: Describes the neural data used in the methods.

claim: The study extracted model responses from layer fc6 which has comparable neural fits to conv5_1 but a lower-dimensional representation.
source: For ease, in all subsequent analyses we use model responses from a con5_1-adjacent layer, fc6, which has comparable neural fits but a lower-dimensional representation.
evidence: Describes a methodological choice.
